---
title: "Reading a .qdpx"
---


You do not need zotQDA to use this package. If your project lives in MAXQDA,
ATLAS.ti, NVivo, QDA Miner or Dedoose, export it as **REFI-QDA** — a `.qdpx`
file — and read that instead:

```r
project <- qda_read_qdpx("my-project.qdpx")
project$fragments      # the same table the CSV exports produce
project$codebook
project$limitations    # what this file cannot support
```

Reading a `.qdpx` needs the suggested package **xml2**
(`install.packages("xml2")`); the rest of qdaR works without it.

Everything downstream then works unchanged, because the frames have the same
columns and the same types as the ones read from CSV.

There is a sample project in the package, so you can try the route before
exporting anything of your own:

```r
p <- qda_read_qdpx(qda_example("sample.qdpx"), warn = FALSE)
qda_code_counts(p$fragments)
qda_agreement(qda_units(p$fragments))
```

## What survives, and what does not

More survives than one might expect. A `.qdpx` carries the code tree with a
**GUID per code** — a stable identity that behaves exactly like `codeId` — the
coders, the timestamps, and the **character positions** of text selections, so
even the unitizing measures work.

What is missing is not a rounding error either.

| | zotQDA CSV exports | a `.qdpx` |
|---|---|---|
| code system: hierarchy, colour, definition | ✓ | ✓ |
| stable code identity across renames | ✓ | ✓ the REFI GUID |
| frequencies, code matrix, code by document | ✓ | ✓ |
| six agreement coefficients with bootstrap intervals | ✓ | ✓ if the export names its coders |
| agreement per code, per hierarchy level, confusion pairs | ✓ | ✓ |
| kappa paradox diagnostics, Wilson intervals | ✓ | ✓ |
| unitizing: α<sub>U</sub>, WindowDiff, Pk, gamma | ✓ | ✓ for text sources |
| chi-squared, Jaccard, scaling, clustering, correspondence analysis | ✓ | ✓ |
| figures in all three backends | ✓ | ✓ |
| multiple-coding report | ✓ | ✓ |
| study planning before data | ✓ | ✓ needs no export at all |
| timeline and saturation | ✓ | ~ additions only |
| coder drift | ✓ | ~ weaker, see below |
| COREQ and SRQR checklists | ✓ | ~ fewer items pre-filled |
| **agreement counting segments nobody coded** | ✓ | ✗ usually absent |
| **crosstabs by author, year, collection or citekey** | ✓ | ✗ |
| **segment weights** | ✓ | ✗ |
| **code abbreviations** | ✓ | ✗ |
| **the three-phase consensus analyses** | ✓ | ✗ |

`qda_read_qdpx()` states which of these apply to **your** file rather than in
general: a project whose codings carry no `creatingUser` cannot support any
agreement coefficient at all, and it says so instead of returning one.

## Why the difference exists

It is not that REFI-QDA is a poor standard. The two formats were designed for
different jobs.

`.qdpx` exists to move a project from one program to another, so it describes
what every program has in common: sources, codes, selections, codings. The
zotQDA exports exist to be analysed, so they carry what an analysis needs and
an interchange format has no reason to include — the bibliographic record
behind each document, a coding log with removals, weights, abbreviations, and
the artefacts of a team consensus procedure.

Three of the gaps are worth understanding rather than merely noting.

**Segments nobody coded.** When two coders both leave a passage alone, they
agree it is irrelevant, and that is agreement. Leaving those segments out
answers a friendlier question: how well the coders agreed *about the material
one of them marked*. REFI has no way to say "here is a passage everyone
considered and passed over", so a coefficient computed from a `.qdpx` is
almost always the friendlier one. See [Agreement](agreement.qmd).

**The coding log.** REFI records when a coding was created and never that one
was withdrawn. Saturation and the timeline read the reconstructed log the same
way as a real one, but a coder who applied and later removed a code looks like
one who never applied it.

**The bibliographic record.** In zotQDA the material *is* a Zotero library, so
every fragment carries its citekey, author and year without anyone entering
them. A `.qdpx` has document names and nothing else.

## What this adds to the program you already use

These packages are not a replacement for MAXQDA or ATLAS.ti, and the
[comparison page](../comparison.qmd) says where those are ahead. But a `.qdpx`
export takes a minute, and it buys numbers and figures your program does not
document.

The claims below are about what each manufacturer's documentation **names**,
surveyed for the comparison page. Absence there is not proof of absence in the
product, and a gap may have been closed since.

### Six things every one of the five is missing

None of the surveyed programs documents any of these:

* **A confidence interval on every agreement coefficient.** Four of the five
  name the coefficients they compute, and not one of those four documents an
  interval — so the figure in most published tables is a point estimate with
  nothing around it. Here every coefficient comes with a seeded percentile
  bootstrap interval, reproducible across all three implementations.
* **The kappa paradox diagnostics.** Prevalence index, bias index and PABAK
  after Feinstein and Cicchetti, plus prevalence with a Wilson interval. This
  is what turns *our kappa was 0.31* into a sentence you can defend, by
  separating a skewed distribution from coders who genuinely differ.
* **Agreement recomputed at every level of the code hierarchy**, plus the
  confusion pairs that cost you the agreement. A disappointing coefficient
  becomes a list of definitions to sharpen.
* **Saturation as a reportable number.** Guest, Namey and Chen's *6+2*
  notation with its base, run and threshold, and the accumulation models of
  Lowe and colleagues for how far from the top you are.
* **Sample-size planning before you collect anything.** How many segments to
  double-code for a kappa interval you can defend (Donner and Rotondi), and how
  many documents to expect a theme of a given prevalence (Fugard and Potts).
* **COREQ and SRQR checklists**, reproduced verbatim and pre-filled where the
  export knows the answer.

### And, specifically for your program

| If you work in | your documentation names | what these packages add on top |
|---|---|---|
| **MAXQDA** | percentage agreement and one kappa; with Analytics Pro also crosstabs with chi-squared, Phi and Cramér's V | Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha and Gwet's AC1 · all four unitizing measures · correspondence analysis, multidimensional scaling, clustering with the cophenetic correlation |
| **ATLAS.ti** | percentage agreement, the Holsti index, and the Krippendorff family including alpha binary | Cohen, Fleiss, Brennan–Prediger and AC1 · WindowDiff, Pk and Mathet's gamma beside alpha binary · the whole inferential set |
| **NVivo** | percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa | four further coefficients · every unitizing measure · the whole inferential set |
| **Dedoose** | Cohen's kappa, pooled and per code | four further coefficients · every unitizing measure · the whole inferential set |
| **QDA Miner / WordStat** | an inter-rater module whose coefficients the public documentation does not name; MDS, correspondence analysis, sequence analysis | six coefficients you can cite by their source, each with an interval · the unitizing measures |

**ATLAS.ti is the closest of the five on the hardest point.** Its alpha binary
asks the same prior question the unitizing measures here do — whether the
coders marked the same stretches at all — and that is a distinction most of the
field still skips.

### The figures

Most of the surveyed programs draw code matrices and co-occurrence tables
perfectly well, so this is a shorter list than the metrics. Four are worth
naming:

* **the level-agreement curve** — where in the code hierarchy the agreement
  breaks down, which no surveyed program offers;
* **the saturation curve** over documents in first-coding order;
* **correspondence and scaling maps that state how much of the structure they
  show** — a map displaying a fifth looks exactly like one displaying nearly
  all of it, so the share travels in the title;
* **the dendrogram with its cophenetic correlation**, which says whether the
  tree is drawing structure the distances actually support.

The general gain is smaller but more useful than any single chart: every figure
is built from a table you can also have on its own, and every one is produced
by a script that still runs next year. A reviewer asking how a number was made
can be handed the file and the code.

::: {.callout-warning title="Read these gains against the limits above"}

From a `.qdpx` the agreement coefficients count only segments somebody
marked, and the saturation curve sees additions but not withdrawals. The
numbers are real; the caveats in the table above travel with them.
:::

## Getting a .qdpx out of your program

All five of the programs surveyed on the [comparison page](../comparison.qmd)
export REFI-QDA; look for *Export → REFI-QDA project* or similar. The standard
itself is documented at [qdasoftware.org](https://www.qdasoftware.org/).

Two practical notes. Export the **project**, not just the codebook: a `.qdc`
holds the code system alone and none of the codings. And if intercoder
agreement is what you are after, check first that your program writes a user
per coding — that single attribute decides whether any of it can be computed.

## If you find the gaps limiting

Then the argument for [zotQDA](https://zotqda.org) is the table above, and the
route back is short: it imports `.qdpx` too, so a project can move in either
direction. What you would gain is the right-hand column becoming the left-hand
one — the coding log, the uncoded segments, the bibliographic metadata and the
consensus procedures.

What you would give up is set out just as plainly on the
[comparison page](../comparison.qmd), which is worth reading before moving
anything.
